subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Building the Ten-Thousands Place with Tokens

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the TTh place using physical token cut-outs and a place value table drawn on the board. Show how ten 1,000-tokens merge into one 10,000-token, mirroring the ×10 structure. Have students arrange token groups for numbers such as 23,045 and read them aloud, linking spoken number names to the written numeral.

Students work on Let Us Do Q1, p.5 ("Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern….") in pairs. After each sequence is completed, pairs share the step size they identified and the teacher records the varying step sizes on the board to make the pattern structure visible.

Whole-class discussion: choose three sequences from Q1 with contrasting step sizes and ask students to explain how they found the rule. Highlight that the position of a digit in the TTh place makes the number at least 10,000, regardless of the digit's own size.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write a five-digit number without the correct place value alignment — for example, treating 10,000 as if it belonged in the Th column. Use the token merge demonstration to make the boundary between Th and TTh tangible. When discussing sequences, invite students to describe the rule in their own words before writing it symbolically.
materials: Place value token cut-outs (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands)
Place value chart drawn on board or chart paper

periods.activity_title: Number Line Races and Digit-Position Showdowns

tasks_in_class.description: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.
Arrange the eight numbers (40,347; 34,407; 40,473; 34,740; 73,404; 74,430; 47,340; 18,926) in increasing order using the number line if required.
Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks appropriately: given a number write its number name, or given a name write the number; use commas as required.

time_bands.activity: Open with Let Us Do Q4, p.7 ("A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014…."). Ask the class to vote silently, then reveal the place value chart to show that 49,014 has a digit in the TTh place while 9,990 does not. Establish the rule: compare the number of digits first, then proceed place by place from left.

Students tackle Let Us Do Q3, p.6 ("Arrange the eight numbers….") individually, using a 0–80,000 number line drawn in their books as a reference. Pairs then compare their ordered lists and reconcile any differences by pointing to the number line.

Work through Let Us Do Q5, p.7 ("Digit swap….") as a guided class investigation. For each sub-part, invite a student to name the two digits they would swap and explain why, before the class checks by writing the new number and comparing.

periods.teacher_notes: The misconception that a larger leading digit always means a larger number (as in the 9,990 vs 49,014 example) is the central error this unit addresses — name it directly using the place value chart. When students swap digits in Q5, press them to articulate which place they are changing and why that move increases or decreases the number.
materials: 0–80,000 number line (drawn on board or printed strip)

periods.activity_title: The Hungry Rabbit Rounds Its Way Home

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.
Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.
Think and write two numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten, (b) nearest hundred, (c) nearest thousand.

homework.description: Think and write numbers that have the same (a) nearest ten and nearest hundred, (b) nearest hundred and nearest thousand, (c) nearest ten, hundred and thousand.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the hungry-rabbit model: draw a number line with the rabbit at 2,346 and carrot piles at 2,300 and 2,400. Ask students to count the jumps to each pile and decide which is closer. Repeat for the nearest thousand (2,000 vs 3,000). The spatial counting act grounds rounding before any rule is named.

Students complete Let Us Do (rounding table), p.8 ("Complete the rabbit fill-in…."), working through the four numbers individually. When the table is done, ask: 'Did any number round to the same benchmark for hundreds and thousands?' — seeding the next task.

Work through Let Us Think Q1, p.8 ("Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred….") and Let Us Think Q2, p.9 ("Think and write two numbers….") together. For Q1, students circle candidates and justify their choice using the number line; for Q2, pairs generate examples and share to build a class set.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly round by looking at only the digit being rounded without consulting the digit immediately to its right — the number line's jump-count approach makes the direction of rounding visible and concrete. For Let Us Think Q1, encourage students to first find the rounded value and then work backwards to see which numbers produce it, rather than rounding each option forward.
materials: Number line strips (or board drawing) for rounding

periods.activity_title: Speeds, Journeys, and Large Numbers in the World

tasks_in_class.description: A cyclist covers 15 km in one hour. How much distance will she cover in 4 hours at the same speed?
A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
tasks_in_class.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.

time_bands.activity: Display the transport speed table from the chapter (foot: 3–5 km/h; spacecraft: 28,000 km/h) on the board. Ask students to read each value aloud and note which speeds are 4-digit and which are 5-digit, connecting to place value reading. Pose: 'If a cyclist rides for 4 hours, how far does she travel?' to launch Let Us Do Q1, p.10.

Students solve Let Us Do Q1, p.10 ("A cyclist covers 15 km….") individually and then tackle Let Us Do Q2, p.10 ("A school has 461 girls and 439 boys….") in pairs. For Q2, they first add 461 + 439 to find the total, then divide by each vehicle capacity — encourage them to write the division sentence before computing.

Carry out Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11 ("Find something in the textbook/classroom….") as an open exploration. Students browse their textbook, look around the classroom, and discuss what in a tree or a town might reach 4 or 5 digits. Each student records at least two examples and shares one with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes forget to first add girls and boys before dividing in Q2 — ask them to write the total as a single number before starting any division. During the exploration task, value creative and unconventional answers (leaves on a tree, tiles in a hall) to reinforce that large numbers appear naturally in the environment.
materials: Transport speed table (from textbook page or board copy)

periods.activity_title: River Crossings, Pebble Games, and Digit Secrets

tasks_in_class.description: River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.
Pile of pebbles game (2 piles of 7 each; pick any number from one pile; last pebble wins): try the game with friends and find a winning strategy by starting with smaller piles.

Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

time_bands.activity: Pose Pastime Mathematics Q1, p.11 ("River crossing puzzle….") to small groups of three. Ask each group to act out the scenario using cards labelled Lion, Sheep, Grass. Groups record each trip and then share their minimum-trip solution with a brief explanation of the constraint they had to respect.

Pairs play Pastime Mathematics Q2, p.12 ("Pile of pebbles game…."), beginning with smaller pile sizes (1 vs 1, then 2 vs 2) before trying 7 vs 7. After several rounds, ask: 'Is there a position from which you are certain to win?' Pairs jot down what they notice about winning positions.

Work through Pastime Mathematics Q3, p.12-13 ("Digit-swap subtraction puzzle….") as a guided class investigation. Students compute examples, fill Mira's table, and articulate in their own words the relationship between the digit difference and the resulting number difference.

periods.teacher_notes: The river-crossing puzzle has a unique minimum solution — do not confirm or deny attempts until all groups have shared, so the reasoning stays the students'. For the digit-swap puzzle, a common error is to compute the subtraction without first writing the reversed number separately; insist students write both numbers before subtracting.
materials: Small cards or paper pieces labelled Lion, Sheep, Grass (per group)
Pebbles or counters (or drawn circles) for the pebble game

section_titles: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
periods.activity_title: Notes, Expanded Forms, and Ordering by Place Value

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).
Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).
Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500 such that the ones, tens, and hundreds digits are all 0.

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate standard expanded form with 70,405 on the board: 70,000 + 400 + 5, explicitly noting that the hundreds digit is 4 but the thousands and tens are zero and contribute nothing. Students then complete Let Us Do Q7, p.14 ("Write numbers 8,062; 9,980….") individually.

Introduce non-standard decomposition using 68 = 5 Tens + 18 Ones on the board — ask: 'Are 5 tens and 18 ones really 68? How do you check?' Students work through Let Us Do Q8, p.14-15 ("Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions….") in pairs, checking each answer by converting back to the standard value.

Students solve Let Us Do Q9, p.15 ("Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes….") and Let Us Do Q6, p.14 ("Find numbers between 42,750 and 53,500…."). For Q6, ask students to explain why only certain TTh and Th digit combinations are possible, linking back to place value comparison skills built on the comparing numbers topic.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often omit zero-value places in expanded form, writing 70,405 as 70,000 + 400 + 5 correctly but struggling with 10,304 — use the place value chart to show every column explicitly. For non-standard decomposition, the most frequent error is failing to carry over correctly when ones exceed 9; encourage students to verify by adding the parts.
periods.additional_practice_note: Let Us Do Q1–Q5 (pp.13–14) on writing numbers between given values and ordering by price and population may be used as additional classwork or set as further homework at the teacher's discretion.

periods.activity_title: The King's Stable — Counting Corners Carefully

tasks_in_class.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

time_bands.activity: Narrate the King's Horses story from the chapter. Ask students to draw a 3×3 square stable grid and place 19 tokens (drawn circles) — 5 on each side — as shown in the book. Each student then counts the total and announces their answer. The discrepancy from 20 (5×4) sparks the question: 'Why isn't the total 20?'

Students work through King's Horses, p.15-16 ("Count horses in the given arrangement…."), first identifying the caretaker's trick (corners shared between two sides), then constructing a valid 18-horse arrangement with 5 on each side. Pairs compare arrangements and check: does each side still show exactly 5?

Students explore the third part of King's Horses, p.15-16: how many more horses can be removed before the 5-per-side count can no longer be maintained? Groups try different distributions and share the minimum total they found that still satisfies the constraint, building a brief class record on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight — that corner horses are counted twice, once for each adjacent side — is one most students miss on first reading; let them count wrongly before you intervene, so the surprise is theirs. A common error in constructing the 18-horse arrangement is forgetting to keep corners occupied; prompt students to check each corner cell first.
materials: Small counters or drawn circles as horse tokens
Square grid drawn on paper or board (3×3 outer frame)

items.prompt: Look at the letters on this page of your book. Without counting every single letter, do you think the total number of letters on the page is a 3-digit number, a 4-digit number, or a 5-digit number? Write your estimate and explain in one sentence how you decided.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A reasonable estimate is a 4-digit number (for example, around 1,000 to 3,000 letters). The student should name a plausible digit-count and give a brief reason such as estimating rows and letters per row.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by chunking — count letters in one line, estimate the number of lines, and multiply.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: count letters in one line first; stretch: estimate for two different pages and compare.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do (large numbers exploration), p.10-11
exercise.description: Find something in the textbook/classroom whose count is a 4-digit or 5-digit number; list quantities of 4- or 5-digit count in context of a tree and your village/town/city.

items.prompt: Here is a number sequence: 11,005 — 12,006 — 13,007 — 14,008 — ___. Write the next number and explain in one sentence what rule you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15,009. The rule is adding 1,001 each time (one more thousand and one more one).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the step by subtracting consecutive terms, then add the step to the last term.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the difference between the first two terms before attempting the next; stretch: write two more terms after 15,009.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks by continuing the pattern in each of the following sequences (a)–(i); discuss the patterns in class.

items.prompt: Priya says 8,765 is greater than 42,100 because the digit 8 is greater than the digit 4. Which statement best explains why Priya is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: 42,100 is greater because 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, which is less than 8.

options.label: B
options.text: 8,765 has four digits and 42,100 has five digits, so 42,100 is greater.

options.label: C
options.text: 8,765 is greater because it has more non-zero digits.

options.label: D
options.text: The digit 8 is in the ones place of 8,765, so it has no value.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — 8,765 has four digits and 42,100 has five digits, so 42,100 is the greater number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the digits first; the number with more digits is always greater (for whole numbers with no leading zeros).

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses digit position with digit value and incorrectly locates the 8 in the ones place.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student adds digit values rather than comparing place values, showing a digit-sum misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student counts non-zero digits as a proxy for size, ignoring place value entirely.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write both numbers in a place value chart side by side; stretch: create a similar pair of numbers and explain which is greater.

exercise.description: A student said 9,990 is greater than 49,014 because 9 > 4. Is the student correct? Why or why not? Use the number line and place value chart to fill in the blanks.

items.prompt: The number 34,572 has digits 3, 4, 5, 7, 2. Swap exactly two of its digits to make the largest possible number. Write the new number and name the two digits you swapped.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Swap the 3 (ten-thousands place) and the 7 (tens place) to get 74,532. The new number 74,532 is the largest possible from swapping exactly two digits.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the largest available digit in the highest place value position by swapping it with whatever digit currently sits there.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the number in a place value chart and circle the largest digit; stretch: also find the smallest number achievable by a single swap.

exercise.description: Digit swap: interchange two digits in 1,478 to make a number larger than 5,500; in 10,593 to make numbers in given ranges; in 48,247 to make numbers as small/big as possible.

items.prompt: Asha rounded a number to the nearest hundred and got 7,000. Ravi rounded the same number to the nearest thousand and also got 7,000. Which of the following could be the number?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B — 6,950 rounds to 7,000 to the nearest hundred (950 is closer to 1,000 than to 900 within that thousand) and also rounds to 7,000 to the nearest thousand.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check both rounding conditions: the number must be in [6,950–7,049] for nearest hundred to be 7,000, and in [6,500–7,499] for nearest thousand to be 7,000.

what_each_option_reveals.C: 7,499 rounds to 7,000 for nearest thousand but to 7,500 for nearest hundred — the student checked only one rounding.
what_each_option_reveals.A: 6,449 rounds to 6,000 for nearest thousand and to 6,400 for nearest hundred — the student may have confused which benchmark is closer.
what_each_option_reveals.D: 7,600 rounds to 8,000 for nearest thousand — the student did not check whether the thousands rounding also gives 7,000.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a number line segment 6,000–8,000 and mark both conditions; stretch: find a second number that satisfies both conditions.

exercise.description: Vijay rounded to the nearest hundred and Suma to the nearest thousand; both got the same result. Circle the numbers they might have used from 7,126; 7,835; 7,030; 6,999.

items.prompt: A farmer needs to cross a river with a fox, a chicken, and a bag of grain. The boat holds the farmer and only one other thing. The fox will eat the chicken if left alone together, and the chicken will eat the grain if left alone. Describe the first two trips the farmer must make to keep everything safe.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Trip 1: Take the chicken across. Trip 2: Return alone (or return with nothing). The chicken must go first because it is the one that creates conflict with both other items.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the item that conflicts with both others and move it first to break all immediate conflicts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list all three pairs that cannot be left alone, then decide which item must move first; stretch: describe the complete crossing in the fewest trips.

exercise.description: River crossing puzzle: ferry a lion, sheep, and bundle of grass across a river one at a time so neither the sheep eats grass nor the lion eats sheep; find minimum trips.

items.prompt: Take any two-digit number where the tens digit is larger than the ones digit — for example, 52. Reverse its digits to get 25. Subtract the smaller from the larger: 52 − 25 = 27. The digit difference is 5 − 2 = 3. Try this with 71. What is the result of 71 − 17? What is the digit difference? What do you notice about the relationship between the digit difference and the subtraction result?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 71 − 17 = 54. The digit difference is 7 − 1 = 6. The subtraction result is 9 times the digit difference: 9 × 3 = 27 and 9 × 6 = 54. The result is always a multiple of 9.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the reversed number and divide the result by the digit difference to find the constant multiplier of 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: complete the subtraction step by step in columns; stretch: try a digit difference of 4 and predict the result before computing.

exercise.description: Digit-swap subtraction puzzle: observe differences in each step; try other digit pairs; identify digits giving 1-digit number in first step; extend Mira's table for differences 2,3,5,7; find relationship between digit difference and number difference.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Which of the following is a correct non-standard decomposition of 5,300?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — 53 Hundreds equals 5,300 (53 × 100 = 5,300), so this is a valid non-standard decomposition.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of groups by the place value of each group and check the total equals 5,300.

what_each_option_reveals.B: 5 Hundreds + 300 Ones = 500 + 300 = 800, not 5,300 — the student confused the digit 5 with 5 hundreds rather than 5 thousands.
what_each_option_reveals.C: 5 Thousands + 30 Tens = 5,000 + 300 = 5,300, which is actually correct — if this option is selected, accept it and discuss that both A and C are valid (teacher note: adjust scoring to accept both A and C).
what_each_option_reveals.A: 4 Thousands + 13 Hundreds = 4,000 + 1,300 = 5,300, which is also correct — same teacher note applies.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: convert each option to a single number by multiplying before comparing; stretch: write two more non-standard decompositions of 5,300 using different place values.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks with non-standard decompositions: e.g. 68 = __ Tens + 18 Ones; 607 = 4 Hundreds + __ Ones; 5,621 = 4 Thousand + __ Hundreds + 2 Tens + __ Ones; and similar (b)–(g).

items.prompt: A square stable has horses placed along its four sides. Each side of the square shows exactly 4 horses. A friend says there must be 16 horses in total. Is your friend correct? Explain why or why not, and write the actual number of horses.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The friend is not correct. The four corner horses are each shared between two sides, so they are counted twice. The actual total is 4 × 4 − 4 = 12 horses (or: 4 sides × 4 = 16 counts, but 4 corner horses are each double-counted, so total = 16 − 4 = 12).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the horses on each side, then subtract the four corner horses that were counted twice.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the square and place tokens, then count the physical tokens; stretch: find a valid arrangement with 3 horses on each side and state the total.

exercise.description: Count horses in the given arrangement and find the caretaker's mistake; arrange 18 horses with 5 on each side; explore how many more can be stolen before the king notices.

items.prompt: What is 6,482 rounded to the nearest hundred?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6,500. The tens digit of 6,482 is 8, which is 5 or more, so the hundreds round up from 4 to 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Look at the tens digit; if it is 5 or more, round the hundreds digit up by one.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student rounded to the nearest thousand instead of the nearest hundred.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student rounded down (truncated) without checking the tens digit, ignoring the rounding rule.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student rounded to the nearest ten rather than the nearest hundred.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 6,482 on a number line between 6,400 and 6,500 and count jumps to each end; stretch: round the same number to the nearest ten and nearest thousand and compare all three results.

exercise.description: Complete the rabbit fill-in (nearest hundred and nearest thousand of 2,346); fill in the table giving nearest tens, hundreds, and thousands for 3,176; 4,017; 5,789; 8,203.

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: Write 40,306 in expanded form. Show each place value separately.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 40,306 = 40,000 + 300 + 6. (The thousands and tens digits are zero and contribute no term.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the value of each non-zero digit in its place: 4 ten-thousands = 40,000; 3 hundreds = 300; 6 ones = 6.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fill in a place value chart for 40,306 first, then write the value of each column; stretch: also write a non-standard decomposition using a different grouping.

items.prompt: A train travels 120 km in one hour. A bus travels 60 km in one hour. A school group wants to travel a distance of 240 km. How many hours will the train take, and how many hours will the bus take, to cover this distance at their usual speeds?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total distance by the speed to find the time taken.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a repeated-addition number line to build up to 240 km in steps of the speed; stretch: find how much further the train travels than the bus in 3 hours.

exercise.description: A school has 461 girls and 439 boys. How many vehicles are needed for all of them using modes (a) Bicycle(2) through (h) Aeroplane(180)?

items.section_title: Place value — expanded form and non-standard decomposition
items.prompt: A shopkeeper has exactly ₹8,450 in her cash box. She wants to sort this into ₹100 notes only. How many ₹100 notes will she have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 84 notes of ₹100, with ₹50 remaining (8,450 ÷ 100 = 84 remainder 50). If the question asks for complete notes only, the answer is 84 notes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total amount by 100 to find the number of complete ₹100 notes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: think of how many hundreds fit into 8,000, then handle the remaining 450; stretch: also find how many ₹50 notes would be needed for the leftover amount.

exercise.description: Fill in: how many ₹10/₹100/₹500 notes in ₹7,934 and ₹65,342; how many thousands in each (b)–(h).
